about: ENGF0003 Mathematical Modelling and Analysis 1 is a 15-credit, Term 1, faculty-wide first-year module in UCL's Integrated Engineering Programme (2026/27 catalogue). It covers estimation, calculus, linear algebra, complex numbers, differential equations, numerical methods and statistics through engineering applications, together with MATLAB modelling and data visualisation, quantitative report writing and ethical, societal and environmental issues. Teaching is flipped: short videos and auto-graded Moodle exercises before hands-on problem-solving classes and workshops. Assessment in 2026/27 is 50% coursework (two assessments) and a 50% invigilated exam; the catalogue says the coursework and a project focus on open-ended, real-life engineering and sustainability problems, and the exam on technical mathematics problems (it does not say exactly how the project fits into the two coursework assessments).
topics: MATLAB computing, modelling and data visualisation
Quantitative report writing and ethical, societal and environmental issues

notes.h: Estimation: orders of magnitude, units and sanity checks
notes.body:
Estimation comes first in ENGF0003's official topic list. Engineers constantly need a quick answer that is roughly right, both to make early design decisions and to check whether a detailed calculation or a MATLAB output is believable.

Fermi estimation
- Break an unknown quantity into factors you can estimate, state each assumption, multiply, and round to one or two significant figures.
- Example: the mass of air in a lecture theatre of about 20 m × 15 m × 6 m. Volume ≈ 1800 m³. With air density ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ at room conditions, the mass is ≈ 2200 kg, i.e. about 2 tonnes (order of magnitude 10³ kg).
- Errors in individual factors often partly cancel, so a chain of rough estimates can still land within a factor of two or three of the truth.

Energy estimates
- Heating water: Q = mcΔT, with c ≈ 4.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water.
- Example: 1 litre (1 kg) from 20 °C to 100 °C needs Q ≈ 1 × 4200 × 80 ≈ 3.4 × 10⁵ J. A 3 kW kettle supplies 3000 J each second, so it takes about 336 000/3000 ≈ 110 s, just under 2 minutes (ignoring heat losses, which make the real time a little longer).
- Keep power (W = J/s) and energy (J, or kWh) distinct: 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ.

Dimensional analysis
- Every valid physical equation is dimensionally consistent: both sides have the same units, and you can only add like with like.
- You can use this to guess the form of a relation. If the period T of a pendulum depends on its length L (m), g (m s⁻²) and the bob mass m (kg), the only combination with units of seconds is √(L/g). Mass cannot appear, because nothing else carries kg to cancel it. So T = k√(L/g); the full theory gives k = 2π for small swings, so a 1 m pendulum has T ≈ 2.0 s.
- Checking units is the fastest way to catch algebra mistakes.

Significant figures and uncertainty
- Quote answers to a precision that matches the data. An estimate built from one-figure assumptions deserves one or two significant figures, not eight.
- For products and quotients, relative (percentage) uncertainties roughly add (worst case). For sums and differences, absolute uncertainties add. Subtracting two nearly equal measured values can leave a huge relative error.
- Use powers of ten and prefixes (k, M, G; m, μ, n) to keep numbers readable.

Sanity checks on models
- Compare a model's output with a quick estimate. Check limiting cases: what happens when a parameter is zero or very large? Check the sign and the trend.

Exam tips: write down every assumption with its value and units, carry units through each line, round sensibly at the end, and add one sentence on whether the answer is plausible.

In ENGF0003 calculus is taught through applications: derivatives describe rates of change and help find optimal designs, and integrals add up quantities such as energy, mass or distance.

Differentiation
- f′(x) is the instantaneous rate of change of f, and the gradient of its graph.
- Rules: product (uv)′ = u′v + uv′; quotient (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²; chain rule d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) g′(x).
- Standard results: d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹; d/dx eᵃˣ = aeᵃˣ; d/dx ln x = 1/x; d/dx sin ax = a cos ax; d/dx cos ax = −a sin ax.

Optimisation
- Stationary points satisfy f′(x) = 0. Classify them with f″ (f″ > 0 minimum, f″ < 0 maximum) or by the sign change of f′. Always check the end points of the allowed range too.
- Example (open box): squares of side x are cut from the corners of a 30 cm × 30 cm sheet and the sides folded up. V = x(30 − 2x)², for 0 < x < 15. Then dV/dx = (30 − 2x)² − 4x(30 − 2x) = (30 − 2x)(30 − 6x), which is zero at x = 5 or x = 15. x = 15 gives V = 0, so the maximum is at x = 5 cm, with V = 5 × 20² = 2000 cm³.
- Example (fixed perimeter): a rectangle with perimeter P and side x has area A = x(P/2 − x), which is maximised at x = P/4, a square, with area P²/16.

Linear approximation
- Near x = a, f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). This is why sin θ ≈ θ (θ in radians) for small angles. It is used to linearise models, for example to simplify a pendulum equation.

Integration
- The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx adds up f over [a, b]; it is the net signed area under the graph.
- Accumulation: energy = ∫ power dt; distance = ∫ velocity dt; mass = ∫ density dV.
- Example: if a machine draws P(t) = 5 + 2t kW for 0 ≤ t ≤ 3 hours, the energy used is ∫₀³ (5 + 2t) dt = 15 + 9 = 24 kWh.
- Average value of f on [a, b]: (1/(b − a)) ∫ₐᵇ f dx. For example, sin t averages 2/π ≈ 0.637 over half a cycle.
- Techniques: substitution (reverse chain rule) and integration by parts, ∫u v′ dx = uv − ∫u′v dx. For example, ∫₀^∞ x e⁻ˣ dx = [−x e⁻ˣ]₀^∞ + ∫₀^∞ e⁻ˣ dx = 1.

Functions of several variables
- Many engineering quantities depend on several inputs, e.g. profit as a function of two prices. Partial derivatives ∂f/∂x and ∂f/∂y measure the change in one input with the other held fixed. Optimisation then needs both to be zero.

Exam tips: define your variable and its allowed range before optimising, justify that a stationary point is a maximum or minimum, carry units through every integral, and check the answer makes physical sense (no negative lengths or volumes).

notes.h: Linear algebra: vectors, matrices and linear systems
notes.body:
Linear algebra is the language for systems with many interacting quantities, such as the forces in a truss, currents in a circuit or flows in a network. ENGF0003 lists linear algebra among its core topics; eigenvalues, Gaussian elimination and matrix factorisations are listed for the follow-on module ENGF0004 (FHEQ Level 5, normally taken in the second year).

Vectors
- A vector has magnitude and direction: a = (a₁, a₂, a₃), with |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²).
- Dot product: a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b| cos θ. It is zero for perpendicular vectors and is used for the work done, W = F · d. Example: (1, 2, 2) · (3, 0, 4) = 11, and the angle between them is arccos(11/15) ≈ 42.8°.
- Cross product: a × b is perpendicular to both, with magnitude |a||b| sin θ (used for moments, M = r × F). Example: (1, 2, 3) × (4, 5, 6) = (−3, 6, −3).

Matrices
- An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. AB is defined when A has as many columns as B has rows.
- Matrix multiplication is not commutative. With A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[0, 1], [1, 0]], AB = [[2, 1], [4, 3]] but BA = [[3, 4], [1, 2]].
- The identity I satisfies AI = IA = A. The transpose Aᵀ swaps rows and columns.

Determinants and inverses
- 2 × 2: det [[a, b], [c, d]] = ad − bc, and the inverse is (1/(ad − bc)) [[d, −b], [−c, a]], which exists only if ad − bc ≠ 0.
- 3 × 3: expand along a row, e.g. det [[2, 0, 1], [1, 3, 2], [1, 1, 1]] = 2(3 − 2) − 0 + 1(1 − 3) = 0, so that matrix is singular.
- det A ≠ 0 if and only if A is invertible.

Linear systems Ax = b
- Example: 2x + y = 5 and x + 3y = 10. det = 6 − 1 = 5, A⁻¹ = (1/5)[[3, −1], [−1, 2]], so x = (1/5)(15 − 10) = 1 and y = (1/5)(−5 + 20) = 3. Check: 2 + 3 = 5 and 1 + 9 = 10.
- If det A ≠ 0 there is exactly one solution, x = A⁻¹b. If det A = 0 there is either no solution or infinitely many, depending on b. Geometrically, two lines either meet once, are parallel, or coincide.
- In practice (and in MATLAB) you solve with A\b rather than forming inv(A), which is slower and less accurate.

Matrices as transformations
- A 2 × 2 matrix maps the plane to itself. The rotation through θ is [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]], and |det| gives the factor by which areas are scaled.

Exam tips: check dimensions before multiplying, verify a solution by substituting it back, and use the determinant to decide whether a unique solution exists before trying to find it.

Complex numbers make oscillations and alternating-current (AC) circuits much easier to handle. Engineers often write j instead of i for √−1, because i is used for current.

Forms of a complex number
- Cartesian: z = x + jy, with real part x and imaginary part y.
- Modulus |z| = √(x² + y²). Argument arg z = θ with tan θ = y/x, in the correct quadrant (atan2(y, x) in MATLAB).
- Polar: z = r(cos θ + j sin θ). Exponential: z = re^(jθ), using Euler's formula e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ.
- Example: z = 3 + 4j has |z| = 5 and arg z = arctan(4/3) ≈ 0.927 rad (53.1°).

Arithmetic
- Add and subtract in Cartesian form. Multiply or divide most easily in polar form: moduli multiply (or divide) and arguments add (or subtract).
- The conjugate z̄ = x − jy satisfies z z̄ = |z|². To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate: 1/(3 + 4j) = (3 − 4j)/25 = 0.12 − 0.16j.
- Examples: (1 + j)(1 − 2j) = 3 − j; (1 + j)/(1 − j) = j; (1 + j)⁸ = (√2)⁸ e^(j2π) = 16.

De Moivre and roots
- (cos θ + j sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + j sin nθ.
- The n-th roots of w = Re^(jφ) are R^(1/n) e^(j(φ + 2πk)/n) for k = 0, 1, …, n − 1. They are equally spaced round a circle.
- Example: z³ = 8 has roots 2, 2e^(j2π/3) = −1 + j√3 and 2e^(−j2π/3) = −1 − j√3.

Phasors and impedance
- A sinusoid A cos(ωt + φ) is the real part of Ae^(jφ)e^(jωt), so it can be represented by the phasor Ae^(jφ). Differentiating with respect to t then becomes multiplying by jω.
- Impedances: resistor Z = R; inductor Z = jωL; capacitor Z = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC). Series impedances add, and V = IZ (Ohm's law with complex numbers).
- Example: R = 1 kΩ in series with C = 1 μF at ω = 1000 rad/s. Z_C = −j/(1000 × 10⁻⁶) = −1000j Ω, so Z = 1000 − 1000j Ω, with |Z| ≈ 1414 Ω and phase −45°. A 10 V amplitude source drives a current of amplitude 10/1414 ≈ 7.07 mA, leading the voltage by 45°.
- Example: R = 10 Ω in series with L = 0.05 H at 50 Hz: ω = 2π × 50 ≈ 314 rad/s, so Z = 10 + 15.7j Ω, with |Z| ≈ 18.6 Ω and phase ≈ 57.5°.

Why this matters
- In the 2020–21 run of the module, complex numbers were taught through microphone design (CEEDA case study). Complex exponentials also appear in the solutions of damped oscillator equations (see differential equations).

Exam tips: draw z on an Argand diagram before quoting an argument, keep angles in radians unless asked otherwise, and remember 1/j = −j when working with capacitors.

A differential equation links a quantity to its rate of change. Most engineering models of change, from cooling and pollution to vibration, are ordinary differential equations (ODEs). In the 2020–21 delivery of ENGF0003 (CEEDA case study) examples included clearing pollution from a lake and an energy-balance model of the climate.

Building a model
- Use a balance: rate of change = rate in − rate out. State assumptions (well mixed, constant parameters) and check units on each term.
- Example (lake pollution): a lake of volume V (m³) has clean inflow and equal outflow Q (m³/day). With concentration c, the pollutant mass is Vc, and V dc/dt = −Qc.

First-order separable equations
- dy/dt = f(t)g(y): separate and integrate, ∫ dy/g(y) = ∫ f(t) dt.
- Lake: dc/dt = −(Q/V)c gives c = c₀e^(−Qt/V). The time constant is V/Q, and the time for c to fall to 10% is (V/Q) ln 10. If V/Q = 50 days, that is about 115 days.
- Newton's law of cooling: dT/dt = −k(T − Tₐ) gives T = Tₐ + (T₀ − Tₐ)e^(−kt). Coffee at 90 °C in a 20 °C room with k = 0.05 per minute is at 20 + 70e^(−0.5) ≈ 62.5 °C after 10 minutes.

First-order linear equations
- dy/dt + p(t)y = q(t). Multiply by the integrating factor e^(∫p dt) so that the left side becomes the derivative of a product.
- Example: dy/dt + 2y = 4 with y(0) = 0. The integrating factor is e^(2t), so (ye^(2t))′ = 4e^(2t), giving ye^(2t) = 2e^(2t) + C, and y = 2 − 2e^(−2t). The solution approaches the steady state 2 with time constant ½.
- Steady states come from setting the derivative to zero. They tell you the long-term behaviour without solving fully.

Second-order linear equations with constant coefficients
- m x″ + c x′ + k x = 0 models a mass–spring–damper. Try x = e^(λt) to get the characteristic equation mλ² + cλ + k = 0.
- c² > 4mk: two real negative roots, overdamped (no oscillation).
- c² = 4mk: repeated root, critically damped: x = (A + Bt)e^(λt).
- c² < 4mk: complex roots λ = −α ± jβ, underdamped: x = e^(−αt)(A cos βt + B sin βt), a decaying oscillation.
- c = 0: undamped simple harmonic motion with ω = √(k/m).
- Example: m = 1, c = 2, k = 5 gives λ² + 2λ + 5 = 0, so λ = −1 ± 2j. With x(0) = 1 and x′(0) = 0: A = 1 and −A + 2B = 0, so B = ½, giving x = e^(−t)(cos 2t + ½ sin 2t).
- With a forcing term on the right-hand side, add a particular solution to this complementary function.

Interpreting solutions
- Check initial conditions, long-term limits and units. Discuss which assumptions limit the model (constant flow, perfect mixing, linear damping).

Exam tips: always state the general solution before applying initial conditions, show the integrating factor or the characteristic equation explicitly, and finish with a sentence interpreting the answer physically.

notes.h: Numerical methods: roots, ODEs and integrals
notes.body:
Most real engineering models cannot be solved exactly, so we compute approximate answers and control their error. ENGF0003 lists numerical methods as a core topic and uses MATLAB to carry them out.

Root finding
- Bisection: if f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs, there is a root in between (intermediate value theorem). Halve the interval each step, keeping the half where the sign changes. After n steps the error is at most (b − a)/2ⁿ, so reaching 10⁻³ on an interval of length 1 needs 10 steps. It is slow but guaranteed.
- Newton–Raphson: x_(n+1) = x_n − f(x_n)/f′(x_n). It follows the tangent line to where it crosses the axis. Near a simple root it converges quadratically (the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step), but it can fail if f′ is near zero or the starting guess is poor.
- Example: √2 as the root of f(x) = x² − 2 from x₀ = 1 gives x₁ = 1.5, x₂ = 1.416 67, x₃ = 1.414 216 (true value 1.414 214).

Euler's method for ODEs
- For dy/dt = f(t, y), step forward along the tangent: y_(n+1) = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n).
- Example: dy/dt = −2y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1. Then y₁ = 1 + 0.1(−2) = 0.8 and y₂ = 0.8 + 0.1(−1.6) = 0.64, compared with the exact value e^(−0.4) ≈ 0.670 at t = 0.2.
- The global error is proportional to h (first order): halving h roughly halves the error.
- Stability: for dy/dt = −2y each step multiplies y by (1 − 2h). If h > 1 then |1 − 2h| > 1 and the numerical solution oscillates and grows even though the true solution decays. With h = 1.5 the values are −2, 4, −8, 16, …
- MATLAB's ode45 uses a more accurate adaptive Runge–Kutta method, but the ideas of step size, error and stability are the same.

Numerical integration
- Trapezium rule with n strips of width h: ∫ f ≈ h[½f₀ + f₁ + … + f_(n−1) + ½fₙ]; error proportional to h². Simpson's rule (n even) has error proportional to h⁴.
- These rules also work directly on measured data, such as power readings taken every 10 minutes, where no formula for f exists.

Errors
- Truncation error comes from the method (e.g. the size of h). Round-off error comes from finite-precision arithmetic.
- Check convergence by repeating with a smaller h or a tighter tolerance and seeing whether the answer settles down.

Exam tips: lay out iterations in a table with enough decimal places, state the stopping criterion, and comment on accuracy (compare with an exact value or a refined computation).

notes.h: Statistics: summarising data and modelling variability
notes.body:
Engineering data always vary: material strengths, measured loads, sensor readings. ENGF0003 lists statistics as a core topic, alongside summarising and visualising data in MATLAB. (Hypothesis tests such as t-tests and ANOVA are listed for the Level 5 follow-on module ENGF0004.)

Summary statistics
- Mean x̄ = (1/n) Σxᵢ. Median: the middle value when the data are sorted (robust to outliers).
- Sample variance s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n − 1); standard deviation s = √s². Dividing by n − 1 rather than n corrects the bias from estimating the mean from the same data.
- Example: 12, 15, 11, 18, 14 have mean 14 and median 14. The deviations −2, 1, −3, 4, 0 have squares summing to 30, so s² = 30/4 = 7.5 and s ≈ 2.74. (Dividing by n instead gives 2.45.)
- Visualise with histograms, box plots and scatter plots before calculating anything.

Probability basics
- Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).
- Reliability: components in series all have to work, so with three components of reliability 0.95 the system reliability is 0.95³ ≈ 0.857. In parallel (redundant) only one needs to work, so for two components it is 1 − 0.05² = 0.9975.

The normal distribution
- X ~ N(μ, σ²) is symmetric and bell-shaped. Standardise with z = (x − μ)/σ and use tables or MATLAB's normcdf.
- About 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.
- Example: concrete strength N(40, 4²) MPa. P(X < 32) = P(Z < −2) ≈ 0.023, so about 2.3% of specimens would fall below 32 MPa.

Fitting a straight line
- The least-squares line y = a + bx minimises the sum of squared vertical residuals: b = Sxy/Sxx and a = ȳ − b x̄, where Sxx = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² and Sxy = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ).
- Example: x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1 give b = 1.99 and a = 0.05.
- The correlation coefficient r = Sxy/√(Sxx Syy) lies between −1 and 1 and measures the strength of a linear relationship (here r ≈ 0.999).
- Cautions: correlation does not imply causation; r near 0 does not rule out a strong non-linear relationship; extrapolating beyond the range of the data is risky; always plot the residuals.

Exam tips: show the formula, the substituted numbers and the result; say whether you used n or n − 1; and add a sentence interpreting the number in its engineering context.

notes.h: MATLAB for modelling, simulation and data visualisation
notes.body:
MATLAB is the computing tool used throughout ENGF0003 to model engineering problems, run simulations and visualise data. A MathWorks case study (undated) describes students on the module completing the MATLAB Onramp tutorial in their first week and doing autograded tasks in MATLAB Grader; check the current arrangements on Moodle.

Basics
- Everything is a matrix. x = [1 2 3] is a row vector; y = [1; 2; 3] is a column vector; A = [1 2; 3 4] is 2 × 2.
- A semicolon at the end of a line suppresses the output. Indexing starts at 1: x(1) is the first element, A(2,1) is row 2, column 1, and x(end) is the last element.
- Ranges: 0:0.1:1 gives 11 points from 0 to 1. linspace(0, 1, 5) gives 5 equally spaced points.
- Element-wise operators have a dot: x.^2, x.*y, x./y. Without the dot, * and ^ mean matrix multiplication and matrix power. For x = [1 2 3], x.^2 is [1 4 9], but x^2 is an error because x is not square.
- A' is the (conjugate) transpose.

Solving problems
- Linear systems: x = A\b solves Ax = b (preferred to inv(A)*b).
- Anonymous functions: f = @(x) x.^2 - 2; then f(3) gives 7. fzero(f, 1) finds a root near 1.
- ODEs: [t, y] = ode45(@(t, y) -0.05*(y - 20), [0 60], 90) simulates Newton's law of cooling over 60 minutes. ode45 is an adaptive Runge–Kutta solver.
- Integrals: trapz(t, P) applies the trapezium rule to sampled data; integral(f, a, b) integrates a function.
- Loops and conditions: for k = 1:n ... end; while ... end; if ... elseif ... else ... end.

Scripts and functions
- A script is a sequence of commands sharing the workspace. A function (function y = name(x) ... end) has its own local variables, inputs and outputs, so it is easier to test and reuse.
- Comment with %. Use clear variable names, and preallocate arrays (y = zeros(1, n)) before filling them in loops.

Visualisation
- plot(x, y), then xlabel, ylabel (with units), title, legend, grid on. hold on overlays several curves.
- scatter for raw data, histogram for distributions, subplot or tiledlayout for several panels, semilogy or loglog for data spanning many orders of magnitude.
- A good figure has labelled axes with units, a legend when there are several series, readable fonts, and a caption that tells the reader what to notice.

Working like an engineer
- Validate a simulation against a case you can solve by hand (for example the exact solution of a linear ODE), test sensitivity to step size and parameters, and keep raw data separate from processed results.

Exam tips: know the difference between element-wise and matrix operators, how to set up an anonymous function for fzero or ode45, and what each line of a short script does. Write code that a marker can follow, with comments.

notes.h: Quantitative reports and ethical, societal and environmental issues
notes.body:
The official ENGF0003 description lists two professional skills alongside the mathematics: writing quantitative reports, and considering ethical, societal and environmental issues through mathematics. The 2026/27 catalogue says the coursework and project focus on open-ended, real-life engineering and sustainability problems, so these skills are assessed directly.

Structure of a quantitative report
- Summary: the question, the approach and the key numerical findings in a few sentences, readable by a non-specialist.
- Introduction: context and why the problem matters.
- Model and assumptions: equations, parameter values with units and sources, and the assumptions you made (for example a well-mixed lake or constant flow), with reasons.
- Method: analytical solution and/or numerical method (step size, tolerance, software).
- Results: figures and tables that answer the question.
- Discussion: interpretation, sensitivity to uncertain parameters, validation against data or hand calculations, and limitations.
- Conclusions and recommendations, tied to the question asked.

Presenting numbers well
- Give units everywhere and round to a precision that matches the data. Do not copy every digit MATLAB prints.
- Quote uncertainty or ranges where they matter, for example "between 100 and 130 days depending on flow rate".
- Figures: labelled axes with units, legends, readable fonts, and a caption saying what to notice. Refer to every figure in the text.
- Write for the audience. Decision-makers need the "so what" and the confidence level, not the algebra, which can go in an appendix.

Ethical, societal and environmental issues
- Models influence decisions that affect people and the environment: flood defences, pollution limits, energy policy, medical devices. A wrong assumption can shift risk onto those least able to bear it.
- Ask: whose interests are represented in the objective function (cost, safety, emissions, equity)? What has been left out? Who bears the risk if the model is wrong?
- Be transparent about uncertainty and limitations, and never present a model as more certain than it is.
- Data ethics: consent and privacy for data about people, and bias in data sets that under-represent some groups.
- Sustainability: life-cycle thinking (materials, energy, end of life), and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (17 goals adopted in 2015) as a framework.
- The Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering's Statement of Ethical Principles, updated in February 2026 and intended for all engineering professionals, sets out five principles: honesty and integrity; responsibility to society; accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication; and responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment.
- The fifth principle is new in 2026. It asks engineers to anticipate wider and emerging consequences of technology (the announcement highlights fast-developing technologies such as AI), including possible misuse and effects on future generations, and to take proportionate precautions where harms could be serious or irreversible. If you meet older material listing four principles, it predates this update.

Using maths to expose issues
- Sensitivity analysis shows which assumptions drive a decision. Comparing scenarios (for example different emission pathways in an energy balance model) makes trade-offs visible. Reporting distributions, not just averages, reveals who is affected by extremes.

Exam and coursework tips: always state assumptions and their consequences, quantify uncertainty, and include at least one paragraph that connects your numbers to their impact on people or the environment.

cards.b: An order-of-magnitude estimate made by splitting an unknown quantity into factors that can be estimated, stating each assumption, and combining them.
Q = mcΔT with c ≈ 4.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. 1 kg from 20 °C to 100 °C needs about 336 kJ.
Every term in a valid physical equation has the same dimensions; quantities can only be added or equated if their units match.
From L, g and m, only √(L/g) has units of time, so T = k√(L/g) (k = 2π for small swings); mass cannot appear.
Sums and differences: add absolute uncertainties. Products and quotients: add relative (percentage) uncertainties.

cards.f: Why not quote eight significant figures?
cards.b: The answer can be no more precise than its least precise inputs; extra digits suggest a false accuracy.
d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) g′(x).

cards.f: Classifying a stationary point with f″
cards.b: f′(a) = 0 and f″(a) > 0: local minimum; f″(a) < 0: local maximum; f″(a) = 0: test inconclusive (look at the sign of f′).

cards.f: Maximum volume of an open box from a 30 cm square sheet
cards.b: V = x(30 − 2x)² is maximised at x = 5 cm, giving V = 2000 cm³.
f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) near x = a; e.g. sin θ ≈ θ for small θ in radians.

cards.b: (1/(b − a)) ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. For sin t over half a cycle it is 2/π ≈ 0.637 of the peak.
∫ u v′ dx = uv − ∫ u′ v dx; e.g. ∫₀^∞ x e⁻ˣ dx = 1.
Energy = ∫ P dt; with P in kW and t in hours the result is in kWh.
a · b = Σ aᵢbᵢ = |a||b| cos θ; zero for perpendicular vectors; work W = F · d.

cards.b: (1/(ad − bc)) [[d, −b], [−c, a]], provided ad − bc ≠ 0.

cards.f: When does Ax = b have a unique solution?
cards.b: Exactly when det A ≠ 0 (A invertible). If det A = 0 there is no solution or infinitely many.
No: in general AB ≠ BA (e.g. swapping columns versus swapping rows).

cards.f: Why use A\b in MATLAB instead of inv(A)*b?
cards.b: Backslash solves the system directly by elimination, which is faster and more accurate than forming the inverse.
[[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]; its determinant is 1, so areas are preserved.
e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ.

cards.b: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments: r₁e^(jθ₁) · r₂e^(jθ₂) = r₁r₂e^(j(θ₁ + θ₂)).
R^(1/n) e^(j(φ + 2πk)/n), k = 0, …, n − 1: n roots equally spaced on a circle of radius R^(1/n).
Z = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC): magnitude 1/(ωC), current leads voltage by 90°.
Z = jωL: magnitude ωL, current lags voltage by 90°.

cards.b: Because i (or I) is used for electric current.

cards.b: mλ² + cλ + k = 0, from trying x = e^(λt).
c² > 4mk overdamped; c² = 4mk critically damped; c² < 4mk underdamped (decaying oscillation); c = 0 undamped.

After n halvings of [a, b] the root is within (b − a)/2ⁿ; needs f continuous with a sign change.

Each step multiplies by (1 − λh); the method is stable only if |1 − λh| ≤ 1, i.e. h ≤ 2/λ.

For a normal distribution, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean.

The mean uses every value but is pulled by outliers; the median (middle value) is robust to outliers.

cards.b: Summary, introduction, model and assumptions, method, results, discussion (validation, sensitivity, limitations), conclusions and recommendations.

cards.b: No more than the input data justify; state units and, where it matters, a range or uncertainty.
Varying uncertain inputs to see how much the outputs and decisions change, revealing which assumptions matter most.

cards.f: Five principles of the Statement of Ethical Principles (Engineering Council and RAEng, February 2026)
cards.b: Honesty and integrity; responsibility to society; accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication; responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment (the new fifth principle).
17 global goals adopted by the United Nations in 2015, often used as a framework for the societal and environmental impact of engineering.

cards.f: What makes a good figure in a report?
cards.b: Labelled axes with units, a legend for several series, readable fonts, a caption saying what to notice, and a reference to it in the text.

questions.q: Using c ≈ 4.2 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, roughly how much energy is needed to heat 1 litre of water from 20 °C to 100 °C, and how long would an ideal 3 kW kettle take?
questions.why: Q = mcΔT = 1 × 4200 × 80 ≈ 336 kJ, and 336 000 J ÷ 3000 J/s ≈ 112 s, about 2 minutes. 420 kJ uses ΔT = 100 K, the final temperature rather than the change. 336 J drops the factor 1000 in kJ, so the time also comes out 1000 times too small. 110 minutes divides correctly but reads the answer, which is in seconds, as minutes.

questions.q: The period T of a simple pendulum might depend on its length L, the gravitational acceleration g and the bob mass m. Which form is dimensionally consistent?
questions.why: L/g has units m ÷ m s⁻² = s², so √(L/g) has units of seconds, as T must. √(g/L) has units s⁻¹, a frequency, not a time. L/g has units s², so it is not a time either. √(mL/g) carries kg^½, and nothing else in the problem can cancel the mass units, so mass cannot appear.

questions.q: Estimate the mass of air in a lecture theatre measuring about 20 m × 15 m × 6 m. State your assumptions and give your answer to a sensible precision.
markScheme: Assumes air density ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ (room temperature and pressure); ignores the volume of seats and people
Quotes about 2 tonnes (order 10³ kg), with one or two significant figures
questions.modelAnswer: Volume ≈ 20 × 15 × 6 = 1800 m³. Assuming air at room temperature and atmospheric pressure has density about 1.2 kg/m³, and ignoring the small volume taken up by seats and people, the mass is about 1800 × 1.2 ≈ 2200 kg. Given the rough dimensions, the sensible answer is 'about 2 tonnes', i.e. of order 10³ kg.

questions.q: Squares of side x cm are cut from the corners of a 30 cm × 30 cm sheet, which is folded into an open box of volume V = x(30 − 2x)². Which value of x maximises V?
questions.why: dV/dx = (30 − 2x)(30 − 6x) = 0 gives x = 5 or x = 15; x = 15 gives V = 0, so the maximum is at x = 5 cm (V = 2000 cm³). x = 15 cm is the other stationary point, but there the box has no base. x = 7.5 cm maximises x(30 − 2x), which forgets to square the base side, so it treats the volume as height times one side length instead of height times base area. x = 10 cm comes from writing the base side as 30 − x instead of 30 − 2x (forgetting that a square is cut from both ends of each side): x(30 − x)² is stationary at x = 10.

questions.q: A machine's power demand rises as P(t) = 5 + 2t kW for 0 ≤ t ≤ 3 hours. How much energy does it use over the three hours?
questions.why: Energy = ∫₀³ (5 + 2t) dt = [5t + t²]₀³ = 15 + 9 = 24 kWh. 11 is P(3), a power in kW, not an energy. 33 multiplies the final power by 3 hours, as if the machine drew 11 kW throughout. 15 counts only the constant 5 kW and ignores the rising part.

questions.q: Show that the average value of V(t) = V₀ sin(ωt) over the half-cycle 0 ≤ t ≤ π/ω is 2V₀/π, and explain why the average over a full cycle is not a useful measure of its size.
markScheme: Over a full cycle the positive and negative halves cancel to give 0, so a measure such as the RMS value (V₀/√2) is used instead
questions.modelAnswer: The half-cycle has length π/ω, so the average is (ω/π) ∫₀^(π/ω) V₀ sin(ωt) dt = (ω/π)(V₀/ω)[−cos(ωt)]₀^(π/ω) = (V₀/π)(1 − (−1)) = 2V₀/π ≈ 0.637V₀. Over a full cycle the positive and negative halves cancel, so the average is 0 even though the signal is far from zero. Engineers therefore use the root-mean-square value, V₀/√2 for a sine wave, to describe its effective size.

questions.q: Solve the system 2x + y = 5, x + 3y = 10.
questions.why: det = 2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5, and x = (3 × 5 − 1 × 10)/5 = 1, y = (2 × 10 − 1 × 5)/5 = 3; check 2 + 3 = 5 and 1 + 9 = 10. x = 3, y = 1 swaps the variables and fails the first equation (6 + 1 ≠ 5). 5/7 and 15/7 come from computing the determinant as ad + bc = 7 instead of ad − bc. x = 2.5, y = 10/3 solves each equation on its own as if the other variable were zero.

questions.q: A is a 3 × 3 matrix with det A = 0. What can you conclude about the system Ax = b?
options: It has either no solution or infinitely many, depending on b
It always has infinitely many solutions
It has no solution for any b
questions.why: A singular matrix cannot be inverted, so there is never a unique solution: for some b the equations are inconsistent and for others there is a whole family of solutions. 'Exactly one solution' is the conclusion for det A ≠ 0. 'Always infinitely many' ignores the inconsistent case. 'No solution for any b' is wrong because b = 0 always has at least the solution x = 0, and in fact infinitely many.

questions.q: For A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]], find A⁻¹ and use it to solve Ax = (5, 10)ᵀ. Verify your answer.
What are the modulus and argument of z = 3 + 4j?
questions.why: |z| = √(9 + 16) = 5 and arg z = arctan(4/3) ≈ 0.927 rad (53.1°). 0.644 rad is arctan(3/4), which swaps the real and imaginary parts. 7 adds the parts directly instead of using Pythagoras. 25 is |z|², the result of forgetting the square root.

questions.q: A 1 kΩ resistor is in series with a 1 μF capacitor at ω = 1000 rad/s. What is the total impedance?
questions.why: Z_C = 1/(jωC) = 1/(j × 1000 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/(0.001j) = −1000j Ω, so Z = 1000 − 1000j Ω (|Z| ≈ 1414 Ω, phase −45°). +1000j forgets that 1/j = −j, which gives the capacitor an inductor's sign. 2000 Ω adds the magnitudes as if both were resistors, ignoring the 90° phase difference. 1000 − 0.001j multiplies by ωC instead of dividing by it, i.e. uses −jωC rather than −j/(ωC).

questions.q: Find all three solutions of z³ = 8 in the form x + jy and describe their positions on an Argand diagram.
markScheme: All lie on the circle |z| = 2, spaced 120° (2π/3) apart, forming an equilateral triangle
questions.modelAnswer: 8 = 8e^(j2πk) for any integer k, so z = 8^(1/3) e^(j2πk/3) = 2e^(j2πk/3), with k = 0, 1, 2 giving distinct roots. k = 0: z = 2. k = 1: 2(cos 2π/3 + j sin 2π/3) = −1 + j√3. k = 2: 2(cos 4π/3 + j sin 4π/3) = −1 − j√3. They lie on the circle of radius 2, 120° apart, at the vertices of an equilateral triangle; the two complex roots are conjugates, as expected for a polynomial with real coefficients.

questions.q: Coffee at 90 °C cools in a 20 °C room according to dT/dt = −0.05(T − 20), with t in minutes. What is its temperature after 10 minutes?
questions.why: The solution is T = 20 + 70e^(−0.05t), so T(10) = 20 + 70e^(−0.5) ≈ 62.5 °C. 54.6 °C is 90e^(−0.5), which lets the coffee cool towards 0 °C instead of room temperature. 55 °C assumes it keeps cooling at its initial rate of 3.5 °C per minute, ignoring the slowing as it approaches room temperature. 135 °C uses e^(+0.5), a sign error that makes the coffee heat up.

questions.q: A mass–spring–damper has m = 1, c = 2 and k = 5 (consistent units). How does it behave after being displaced and released?
options: Undamped: it oscillates for ever with constant amplitude
Critically damped: the fastest return without oscillation
Overdamped: it returns to rest without oscillating
questions.why: c² − 4mk = 4 − 20 < 0, so the roots −1 ± 2j are complex with negative real part, giving e^(−t)(A cos 2t + B sin 2t), an oscillation that decays. Overdamped needs c² > 4mk, which comes from reversing the inequality. Undamped needs c = 0; complex roots alone do not mean constant amplitude, because the real part −1 makes it decay. Critically damped needs c² = 4mk, i.e. c = 2√5 ≈ 4.47, not c = 2.

questions.q: Solve dy/dt + 2y = 4 with y(0) = 0. State the steady-state value and the time taken to reach 95% of it.
markScheme: Integrate: y e^(2t) = 2e^(2t) + C, so y = 2 + Ce^(−2t)
Steady state y = 2 (set dy/dt = 0 or let t → ∞)
questions.modelAnswer: The integrating factor is e^(∫2 dt) = e^(2t). Multiplying through gives d/dt(y e^(2t)) = 4e^(2t), so y e^(2t) = 2e^(2t) + C and y = 2 + Ce^(−2t). From y(0) = 0, C = −2, so y = 2(1 − e^(−2t)). As t → ∞, y → 2, the steady state (also found by setting dy/dt = 0 in 4 − 2y = 0). y reaches 95% of 2 when e^(−2t) = 0.05, i.e. t = ½ ln 20 ≈ 1.50.

questions.q: Newton–Raphson is applied to f(x) = x² − 2 starting from x₀ = 1. What is x₂?
questions.why: x₁ = 1 − (1 − 2)/2 = 1.5 and x₂ = 1.5 − (2.25 − 2)/3 = 1.4167. 1.5 is x₁, after only one iteration. 1.25 is the second midpoint you would get from bisection on [1, 2], a different method. 1.4142 is √2 itself; Newton gets close quickly, but x₂ has not yet reached it.

questions.q: Euler's method with h = 0.1 is applied to dy/dt = −2y, y(0) = 1. What is the approximation to y(0.2)?
questions.why: y₁ = 1 + 0.1(−2 × 1) = 0.8, then y₂ = 0.8 + 0.1(−2 × 0.8) = 0.64. 0.6703 is the exact value e^(−0.4), not the Euler estimate. 0.8 is the value after only one step (t = 0.1). 0.6 reuses the initial slope −2 for both steps instead of re-evaluating the slope at y₁.

questions.q: Euler's method is used on dy/dt = −2y, y(0) = 1, with step h = 1.5. Compute the first three steps, explain what goes wrong, and state the largest step size for which the numerical solution does not grow.
markScheme: y₁ = −2, y₂ = 4, y₃ = −8: oscillating and growing
True solution e^(−2t) decays monotonically to 0, so the method is unstable here
questions.modelAnswer: Euler gives y_(n+1) = y_n + h(−2y_n) = (1 − 2h)y_n. With h = 1.5 the factor is −2, so y₁ = −2, y₂ = 4, y₃ = −8: the numerical solution flips sign and doubles every step. The true solution e^(−2t) decays smoothly to zero, so the method is numerically unstable at this step size. The amplification factor must satisfy |1 − 2h| ≤ 1, i.e. 0 < h ≤ 1, for the numerical solution not to grow (and h < 0.5 avoids the sign oscillation altogether).

questions.q: What is the sample standard deviation of the data 12, 15, 11, 18, 14?
questions.why: The mean is 14, the squared deviations sum to 30, and s = √(30/4) = √7.5 ≈ 2.74. 2.45 divides by n = 5 instead of n − 1 = 4, which gives the population standard deviation. 7.5 is the sample variance, before taking the square root. 6 is the population variance (30/5).

questions.q: Concrete cube strengths are modelled as normal with mean 40 MPa and standard deviation 4 MPa. What is the probability that a cube has strength below 32 MPa?
questions.why: z = (32 − 40)/4 = −2, and P(Z < −2) ≈ 0.023. 0.309 comes from dividing by the variance 16 instead of the standard deviation 4, giving z = −0.5. 0.046 is the probability of being more than 2 standard deviations from the mean in either direction, double the one-sided answer. 0.977 is P(X > 32), the wrong tail.

questions.q: A pumping station uses three pumps in series, each working independently with probability 0.95. (a) Find the reliability of the system. (b) The design is changed to two pumps in parallel (redundant). Find the new reliability and comment.
markScheme: (b) Parallel: fails only if both fail: 1 − 0.05² = 0.9975
Comment: redundancy greatly increases reliability; series systems are only as good as the product of their parts (assumes independence)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) In series every pump must work, so R = 0.95³ ≈ 0.857. (b) In parallel the system fails only if both pumps fail, which has probability 0.05² = 0.0025, so R = 1 − 0.0025 = 0.9975. Redundancy raises reliability from about 86% to over 99.7%. The calculation assumes the pumps fail independently; a common cause such as a power cut would make the real reliability lower.

questions.q: In MATLAB, x = [1 2 3]. Which expression gives [1 4 9]?
questions.why: The dot makes the power act on each element, so x.^2 is [1 4 9]. x^2 is a matrix power, which needs a square matrix, so it gives an error for a 1 × 3 row vector. x*x is a matrix product of two 1 × 3 matrices, which fails because the inner dimensions do not match. x'*x is a column times a row, which gives a 3 × 3 matrix (the outer product), not a vector.

questions.q: In MATLAB, A is a square matrix and b is a column vector. Which command solves Ax = b?
questions.why: A\b ('left division') solves Ax = b. b\A solves b x = A, the wrong way round. A*b multiplies A by b instead of solving for x. The expression b/A uses right division, which solves xA = b for a row vector x; with b a column vector the dimensions do not match.

questions.q: Write MATLAB code that uses ode45 to simulate Newton's law of cooling, dT/dt = −0.05(T − 20), for coffee starting at 90 °C over 0 ≤ t ≤ 60 minutes, and plots the result with suitable labels. State what the curve should look like.
markScheme: Defines the right-hand side as an anonymous function, e.g. f = @(t,T) -0.05*(T - 20)
plot(t, T) with xlabel('Time (min)'), ylabel('Temperature (°C)'), title and grid
Describes the expected curve: exponential decay from 90 °C towards 20 °C (about 62.5 °C at 10 min), never going below 20 °C
questions.modelAnswer:
f = @(t, T) -0.05*(T - 20);      % rate of change
[t, T] = ode45(f, [0 60], 90);    % simulate 0 to 60 min from 90 °C
plot(t, T, 'LineWidth', 1.5)
xlabel('Time (min)'); ylabel('Temperature (°C)')
title('Cooling coffee: Newton''s law of cooling'); grid on

The curve should fall steeply at first and then level off, decaying exponentially towards the room temperature of 20 °C (about 62.5 °C after 10 minutes and about 23.5 °C after 60 minutes), matching T = 20 + 70e^(−0.05t).

questions.q: Your MATLAB model predicts that a lake will take 115.129254649 days to clear, using flow rates known to about ±10%. How should you report this?
options: 115.129254649 days, to show the precision of the calculation
115.129254649 days, with no assumptions, so the summary stays short for non-specialists
Exactly 4 months, as non-specialists find months easier
About 115 days, with a stated range (e.g. roughly 105–130 days) and the assumptions listed
questions.why: The inputs are known only to about 10%, so the answer should be rounded and given with a plausible range and the assumptions that drive it. Quoting every digit shows the computer's precision, not the model's accuracy. Leaving out assumptions hides exactly what a decision-maker needs to judge the result. 'Exactly 4 months' converts the units but adds false certainty, and 4 months is not the same as 115 days.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five principles in the Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering Statement of Ethical Principles (February 2026 update)?
options: Responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment
questions.why: The five principles are honesty and integrity; responsibility to society; accuracy and rigour; leadership and communication; and responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment. Profitability and efficiency may matter to a business, but they are not ethical principles in the statement, so that is the answer. Responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment is the new fifth principle added in 2026, so anyone relying on the older four-principle version might wrongly pick it. Honesty and integrity, and leadership and communication, are in both the old and new versions.

questions.q: Using an example of an engineering model (for instance a flood-risk or air-pollution model), explain how modelling assumptions can raise ethical, societal or environmental issues, and how a report should address them.
markScheme: Identifies a concrete model and at least one key assumption (e.g. historical rainfall, average exposure)
Explains a consequence: risk may be underestimated or unevenly distributed, affecting particular groups or the environment
Mentions uncertainty: decisions based on a single best estimate can mislead
Report should state assumptions, quantify uncertainty/sensitivity and present ranges or scenarios

Links to professional responsibility (e.g. accuracy and rigour; responsibility to society; responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment) or to transparency for non-specialist decision-makers
questions.modelAnswer: Consider a flood-risk model used to decide where to build defences. If it is calibrated only on historical rainfall, it may underestimate future extremes under climate change, so the defences could be under-designed. If it uses average property values to compare costs and benefits, it may favour protecting wealthier areas, shifting risk onto poorer communities. Both are mathematical choices with ethical consequences. A good report states such assumptions explicitly, runs sensitivity analyses or scenarios (for example different rainfall projections), presents results as ranges rather than single numbers, and explains in plain language who is affected and how confident the conclusions are. This reflects the principles of accuracy and rigour and responsibility to society in the Engineering Council and RAEng Statement of Ethical Principles (2026), and lets decision-makers weigh the trade-offs openly.

questions.q:
A lake has volume V = 2 × 10⁶ m³. River water flows in and out at the same rate Q = 4 × 10⁴ m³ per day, and the lake is assumed to be well mixed. Initially the pollutant concentration is c₀ = 5 mg/L (= 5 g/m³).
(a) If the inflow is clean, derive and solve the differential equation for c(t), and find how long it takes the concentration to fall to 0.5 mg/L. [6]
(b) Now suppose a factory also discharges the pollutant directly into the lake at a constant 20 kg per day. Write down the new differential equation, find the steady-state concentration, and solve for c(t) with c(0) = 5 mg/L. [7]
(c) In case (b), how long does it take for c to fall to 1 mg/L? [2]
(d) Use one step of Euler's method with h = 10 days to estimate c(10) in case (b), and compare with the exact value. [3]
(e) State two assumptions of the model and how relaxing them might change the conclusions. [2]
markScheme: (a) Mass balance d(Vc)/dt = −Qc, so dc/dt = −(Q/V)c with V/Q = 50 days; c = 5e^(−t/50)
(b) V dc/dt = m − Qc with m = 2 × 10⁴ g/day; steady state c* = m/Q = 0.5 g/m³ = 0.5 mg/L
(b) Solution c = 0.5 + 4.5e^(−t/50) (by separation or integrating factor)
(d) dc/dt at t = 0: (2 × 10⁴ − 4 × 10⁴ × 5)/(2 × 10⁶) = −0.09 mg/L per day; c(10) ≈ 4.1; exact 0.5 + 4.5e^(−0.2) ≈ 4.18; Euler overestimates the drop (first-order error)
(e) e.g. well mixed (real lakes stratify, so some zones clear more slowly); constant flow (seasonal flow changes alter V/Q); no decay or sedimentation (would speed removal)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The pollutant mass is Vc. With clean inflow, mass leaves only in the outflow, at rate Qc, so V dc/dt = −Qc, i.e. dc/dt = −(Q/V)c. Here V/Q = 2 × 10⁶/4 × 10⁴ = 50 days. Separating variables gives c = c₀e^(−t/50) = 5e^(−t/50) mg/L. Setting c = 0.5 gives e^(−t/50) = 0.1, so t = 50 ln 10 ≈ 115 days.

(b) Now mass also enters at m = 20 kg/day = 2 × 10⁴ g/day: V dc/dt = m − Qc, i.e. dc/dt = (m − Qc)/V. Setting dc/dt = 0 gives the steady state c* = m/Q = 2 × 10⁴/4 × 10⁴ = 0.5 g/m³ = 0.5 mg/L. Writing u = c − c*, du/dt = −(Q/V)u, so u = u₀e^(−t/50) with u₀ = 5 − 0.5 = 4.5. Hence c(t) = 0.5 + 4.5e^(−t/50) mg/L.

(c) 1 = 0.5 + 4.5e^(−t/50) gives e^(−t/50) = 1/9, so t = 50 ln 9 ≈ 110 days.

(d) At t = 0, dc/dt = (2 × 10⁴ − 4 × 10⁴ × 5)/(2 × 10⁶) = −1.8 × 10⁵/2 × 10⁶ = −0.09 mg/L per day. Euler gives c(10) ≈ 5 + 10(−0.09) = 4.1 mg/L. The exact value is 0.5 + 4.5e^(−0.2) ≈ 4.18 mg/L. Euler overestimates the fall, because it uses the steepest (initial) slope over the whole step; its error is first order in h, so a smaller step would do better.

(e) The lake is assumed to be well mixed: real lakes can stratify, so parts of the lake may stay polluted much longer than predicted. The flows are assumed constant: in a dry season Q falls, V/Q rises and clearance slows. The pollutant is also assumed not to decay, settle or be taken up biologically; including such losses would speed clearance. Any of these could change whether regulators would accept the predicted time scale.

questions.q:
(a) Six concrete cubes from a batch have strengths (MPa) 36, 40, 42, 38, 44, 40. Calculate the sample mean and sample standard deviation. [4]
(b) Assuming strengths are normally distributed with the mean and standard deviation from (a), estimate the proportion of cubes with strength below 35 MPa. [4]
(c) At five roadside sites, daily traffic flow x (thousands of vehicles) and mean NO₂ concentration y (μg/m³) are:
x: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
y: 21, 26, 33, 36, 44
Find the least-squares regression line y = a + bx and the correlation coefficient r. [8]
(d) Use the line to predict y at x = 7 and at x = 60, and comment on the reliability of each prediction and on whether the data show that traffic causes the NO₂. [4]
markScheme: (d) x = 7: y ≈ 34.8 μg/m³, interpolation, reliable given r ≈ 0.99; x = 60: y ≈ 183, extrapolation far outside data, unreliable
(d) Correlation does not prove causation (confounders such as road layout, wind, other sources); only 5 sites
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Mean = (36 + 40 + 42 + 38 + 44 + 40)/6 = 240/6 = 40 MPa. Deviations: −4, 0, 2, −2, 4, 0, with squares 16, 0, 4, 4, 16, 0 summing to 40. Sample variance s² = 40/(6 − 1) = 8, so s = √8 ≈ 2.83 MPa.

(b) z = (35 − 40)/2.83 ≈ −1.77. From tables, P(Z < −1.77) ≈ 0.038, so about 4% of cubes would be expected to fall below 35 MPa. (With only six cubes the estimates of μ and σ are themselves uncertain, so this is a rough figure.)

(c) x̄ = 30/5 = 6 and ȳ = 160/5 = 32. Deviations in x: −4, −2, 0, 2, 4, so Sxx = 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40. Deviations in y: −11, −6, 1, 4, 12, so Syy = 121 + 36 + 1 + 16 + 144 = 318. Sxy = (−4)(−11) + (−2)(−6) + 0(1) + 2(4) + 4(12) = 44 + 12 + 0 + 8 + 48 = 112.
b = Sxy/Sxx = 112/40 = 2.8 and a = ȳ − b x̄ = 32 − 16.8 = 15.2, so y = 15.2 + 2.8x.
r = Sxy/√(Sxx Syy) = 112/√(40 × 318) = 112/√12 720 ≈ 0.993, a very strong positive linear association.

(d) At x = 7: y ≈ 15.2 + 19.6 = 34.8 μg/m³. This is interpolation within the data range and, with r ≈ 0.99, reasonably reliable. At x = 60: y ≈ 15.2 + 168 = 183.2 μg/m³. This extrapolates six times beyond the largest observed flow, where congestion, road design and dispersion may behave quite differently, so it should not be trusted. The strong correlation is consistent with traffic contributing to NO₂, but it does not prove causation: busier roads may also be in more built-up areas with poorer dispersion or other sources, and five sites is a very small sample. A controlled study or physical dispersion model would be needed to establish cause.
